Arch Dis Child 1997; 76: 356–8. Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease results from the reflux of gastric or duodenal contents into the oesophagus. Symptoms include heartburn, acid regurgitation, and dys- phagia (difficulty in swallowing); oesophageal inflamma- tion and ulceration (reflux oesophagitis), and stricture for- mation may occur. Extra-oesophageal symptoms may include cough, horseness, and asthma. Some patients de- velop Barrett’s oesophagus (below), which is a risk factor for oesophageal cancer (p.664). Lifestyle advice on weight loss, raising the head of the bed, stopping smoking, and avoidance of alcohol and aggravat- ing foods such as chocolate and coffee is often given as part of initial management,1-5 although the evidence for most of these interventions other than weight loss and bed position is lacking.3 Patients often manage initial mild symptoms with over- the-counter therapies, including antacids and antisecretory drugs. Although the placebo response is often high, meta- analysis has shown some additional symptomatic benefit from antacids, histamine H2-antagonists, and in particular for combinations of an antacid with an alginate;6 such combinations are believed to form an alkaline ‘raft’ above the stomach contents that impedes reflux and protects the oesophageal mucosa. The symptoms and management of gastro-oesophageal re- flux disease may overlap with those of dyspepsia (see above), and initial symptomatic management is likely to be similar.4 Patients who do not have alarm symptoms that would indicate a need for prompt endoscopy should be treated with an appropriate dose of a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) for 1 to 2 months.4,5 Such treatment is more effective for empirical management than an H2-antagonist,7 and is appropriate therapy for endoscopy-negative disease7 as well as for patients with reflux oesophagitis.8 There is no evidence for the superiority of any particular PPI, nor for greater benefit from doubling doses in patients with reflux oesophagitis.7 A significant minority of patients do not, however, re- spond to PPIs; reasons may include poor compliance, noc- turnal acid breakthrough, non-acid reflux, and hypersensi- tivity to acid.4,5 Trying an alternative PPI or increasing the dose has been suggested4 (despite the lack of evidence to support this7).
